outputs.final_proof:
\begin{proof}
Let n_{19} and n_{17} denote the numbers of Sylow 19- and 17-subgroups, respectively. Sylow's theorems give
\[
n_{19}\mid153,\quad n_{19}\equiv1\pmod{19},
\]
so n_{19}\in\{1,153\}, and
\[
n_{17}\mid171,\quad n_{17}\equiv1\pmod{17},
\]
so n_{17}\in\{1,171\}.

If either n_{19}=1 or n_{17}=1, the corresponding Sylow subgroup is unique and therefore normal. It remains to rule out n_{19}=153 and n_{17}=171 simultaneously. In that case, the Sylow 19-subgroups contain 153\cdot(19-1)=2754 distinct nonidentity elements, and the Sylow 17-subgroups contain 171\cdot(17-1)=2736 distinct nonidentity elements. A subgroup of order 17 intersects a subgroup of order 19 trivially, so these two collections of nonidentity elements are disjoint. This would give at least 5490 nonidentity elements, contradicting |G|-1=2906.

Therefore at least one Sylow subgroup is unique and normal. Hence G is not simple.
\end{proof}

outputs.final_proof:
\begin{proof}
Since |G|=3^2\cdot17\cdot19, let n_{19} be the number of Sylow 19-subgroups. By Sylow's theorems,
\[
n_{19}\equiv1\pmod{19},\qquad n_{19}\mid153,
\]
hence n_{19}=1 or 153. In the first case, the Sylow 19-subgroup is normal.

Assume n_{19}=153. Let n_{17} be the number of Sylow 17-subgroups. Then
\[
n_{17}\equiv1\pmod{17},\qquad n_{17}\mid171,
\]
so n_{17}=1 or 171. If n_{17}=1, the Sylow 17-subgroup is normal. If n_{17}=171, then distinct Sylow 19-subgroups intersect trivially and contribute 153\cdot18=2754 nonidentity elements. Distinct Sylow 17-subgroups also intersect trivially and contribute 171\cdot16=2736 nonidentity elements. Moreover, a subgroup of order 17 and one of order 19 have trivial intersection. Thus G would contain at least 2754+2736>2906 nonidentity elements, impossible.

Consequently, G has a unique Sylow 19-subgroup or a unique Sylow 17-subgroup. In either case G has a nontrivial proper normal subgroup, and therefore G is not simple.
\end{proof}
